Heaps in Depth

The smallest value always waits on top. Watch values sift up and down, build a heap in linear time, sort with it, guard the top k of a stream, merge sorted lists, track a running median with two heaps and schedule meeting rooms.

Part 1

⛰️Sift up and sift down, step by step

The Trees chapter showed that a min heap keeps the smallest value at the root and lives in a plain array. Two moves keep it in order. Sift up: a new value joins at the end and swaps with its parent while the parent is bigger. Sift down: after the root is removed, the last value jumps to the top and swaps with its smaller child until both children are bigger.

left = 2i + 1   right = 2i + 2   parent = ⌊(i − 1) / 2⌋
A heap of n values has about log₂ n levels, so one push or one pop costs at most O(log n) swaps.
Part 2

🏗️Building a heap in O(n)

Pushing n values one by one costs O(n log n). There is a faster way. Put all values in the array as they are. Every leaf is already a tiny heap. Then sift down each parent, starting from the last parent and moving to the root. Most nodes sit near the bottom and move only a step or two, so the total is O(n).

For 1023 values in the worst order, bottom up needs 1013 swaps while pushing one by one needs 8194. Python's heapq.heapify uses the bottom up method.
Part 3

📶Heap sort

Build a max heap in O(n). The biggest value is now at index 0. Swap it with the last value, treat the array as one shorter, and sift the new root down. The biggest values collect at the end, already in order. Repeat n − 1 times.

Heap sortMerge sortQuick sort
Worst caseO(n log n)O(n log n)O(n²)
Extra memoryO(1)O(n)O(log n)
Stablenoyesno
Part 4

🏅Top k with a small heap

To keep the 3 highest scores from a stream of millions, you do not need to store them all. Keep a min heap of size k. Its root is the smallest of your top k. A new score that is not bigger than the root cannot make the list, so it is ignored at once. A bigger one replaces the root.

For the k largest use a min heap. For the k smallest use a max heap. The root guards the door, and each check costs O(log k).
Part 5

🔀Merging k sorted lists

Several sorted lists need to become one sorted list. The next value is always one of the current heads. Put every head in a min heap, pop the smallest, and push the next value from the same list. With N values in k lists, that is O(N log k).

Databases and search engines merge sorted runs from disk this way when the data does not fit in memory. Python ships it as heapq.merge.
Part 6

⚖️The running median with two heaps

Numbers keep arriving and you want the median after each one. Split them into two halves. The smaller half lives in a max heap, so its biggest is on top. The bigger half lives in a min heap, so its smallest is on top. Keep the halves the same size, or the smaller half one bigger. The median sits right at the two tops.

Part 7

🚪Scheduling: how many rooms?

Meetings have start and end times. How many rooms are needed? Sort the meetings by start. Keep a min heap of the times when each busy room becomes free. For each meeting, if the earliest free time is not after its start, reuse that room. Otherwise open a new one. The heap size at the end is the answer.

Operating systems, printers and game engines all use priority queues like this to decide what runs next. Dijkstra's shortest paths, in the Advanced graphs chapter, uses one too.
